title: Master Class | Will Danish be accepted!? | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Over a thousand this time — let's go. e4, e5.
d4 — the Danish Gambit. We still haven't managed to get one accepted; nobody seems willing to grab the pawn.
Sure enough, Black declines and develops the knight to c6 instead.
I haven't given you much choice — it's not the knight to f3 here, it's d takes e5, clarifying the center.
Black recaptures, the knight to e5. It looks like we're letting Black plant a knight in the center, but that knight has no stable home — it'll have to move again.
We play an inoffensive developing move, the knight to c3, and see how Black arranges his pieces before we commit to f4.
Black develops the knight to f6.
Now f4 — both knights are stuck in no man's land, so we just push and kick them around.
The e5-knight has to retreat, and it goes back to c6 — the jump to g4 would be a disaster.
e5, and now the f6-knight has only one reasonable square.
It's forced all the way back to g8. We have a big center, a big development lead, and Black's king is slightly loosened.
We finish developing with the knight to f3 — no need for anything crazy.
d6 is exactly what Black should do, challenging our center — and these players are starting to play a bit better.
The bishop to c4 is tempting, but the move is the bishop to b5, pinning the knight.
Black breaks the pin with the bishop to d7.
We don't have to do anything fancy — just castle, and look at that f-file, where the disaster is going to unfold for Black.
Black takes on e5, and we recapture with the f-pawn — no reason to take with the knight and trade off pieces that help Black defend.
Black plays the queen to e7, but he's in huge trouble: the e5-pawn cramps him and the open f-file is disastrous.
The knight leaps to d5, threatening the knight to c7 — a devastating fork of the king and rook.
Black checks with the queen to c5. Players are much better at spotting a tactical pattern than at calculating it deeply.
They get attracted to grabbing the bishop — so we block the check with the bishop to e3, hitting the queen.
He finds the best defense, the knight to d4, trying to unpin himself with tempo.
We take on d7 with the bishop, check.
Black recaptures with the king. There are several options — the queen takes d4, simply up a piece in the endgame.
But there's a subtlety: from f2 the bishop could get hit by the knight to f5, then the bishop to d4 walks into the knight to e3 unpinning with check — you have to see that trap before it bites.
The key idea: when your opponent's king sits on the same file as your queen, no matter how many pieces are wedged between them, that alignment should always be factored in.
The knight drops back to c3 — I love these moves; it keeps our forces trained on that d-file where the king lingers.
Black brings the rook to d8.
We take with the bishop on d4 — and there's something sexy here, because it sets up a discovered check.
Black plays the queen to c6.
e6, check — and it's a fork: the pawn hits the king and clears lines all at once, exactly the pattern my brain screams at.
Black takes, f takes e6.
The knight to e5, check — a thematic square-clearing shot that forks the king and the queen, and that's the game.
Black steps the king to c8, and the knight captures the queen, taking on c6.
Black recaptures, b takes c6.
Playing precisely, the rook takes on f8, snapping off a piece.
Black recaptures on f8.
The bishop takes on g7 — and now we're going to pick up a rook.
Black tries to salvage things with the rook to d8.
The cleanest finish runs the queen to d2, the king to b7, the queen to h6, and if the knight takes on h6 we simply mop up — it's crushing.
The bishop takes on h8, and Black is completely lost; he'll resign.
